Craig Lindner
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Excluding the impact of alternative investments, net investment income and our P&C insurance operations for the three months ended 31 March 2024, increased by 16% year-over-year as a result of the impact of higher interest rates and higher balances of invested assets. As you'll see on slide 6, approximately 68% of our portfolio is invested in fixed maturities. In the current interest rate environment, we're able to invest in fixed maturity securities at yields of approximately 6%. Current reinvestment rates compare favorably to the nearly 5% yield earned on fixed maturities in our P&C portfolio during Q1 2024. The duration of our P&C fixed maturity portfolio, including cash and cash equivalents, was 2.9 years at 31 March 2024.
We've strategically managed duration to take advantage of market opportunities as interest rates have increased from recent historic lows. The annualized return on alternative investments in our P&C portfolio was approximately 9% for the 2024 Q1, compared to 14.2% for the prior year quarter. Strong returns related to our traditional private equity portfolio were offset by lower returns on investments tied to multifamily housing, which represent about half of our alternative investment portfolio, and where we continue to experience headwinds from the impact of increased supply and the leveling out of rental rates on these investments. We expect these headwinds may continue throughout the remainder of 2024.
Longer term, we remain optimistic regarding the prospects of our investments in multifamily housing, as these properties continue to generate strong net operating income and have desirable geographic positioning and high occupancy rates. The average annual return on alternative investments over the 5 calendar years ended 31 December 2023 was approximately 13%. Please turn to slide 7, where you'll find a summary of AFG's financial position at 31 March 2024. During the quarter, we returned $269 million to our shareholders through the payment of our regular $0.71 per share quarterly dividend, as well as a $2.50 per share special dividend.
We expect our operations to continue to generate significant excess capital throughout the remainder of 2024, which provides ample opportunity for additional special dividends or share repurchases over the next year. We continue to view total value creation as measured by growth and book value, plus dividends, is an important measure of performance over the long term. For the three months ended 31 March 2024, AFG's growth in book value per share, excluding AOCI, plus dividends, was 5.1%. I'll now turn the call back over to Carl to discuss the results of our P&C operations.
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Thank you, Craig. Please turn to slides 8 and 9 of the webcast, which include an overview of our Q1 results. As you'll see on slide 8, our Specialty Property and Casualty Insurance businesses generated a strong 90.1 combined ratio in Q1 2024, about a point higher than the 89.2 reported in Q1 last year. Results for 2024 Q1 included 2.3 points of catastrophe losses, compared to 2.2 points in last year's Q1, and 3.3 points of favorable prior year reserve development, compared to 4.5 points in Q1 2023. Q1 2024 gross and net written premiums were both up 8% when compared to the same period last year.
Year-over-year growth was reported within each of the Specialty Property and Casualty groups as a result of additional crop premiums from Crop Risk Services acquisition, new business opportunities, increased exposures, and a good renewal rate environment. Along those lines, average renewal pricing across our Property and Casualty group, excluding our workers' comp businesses, was up 8% for the quarter, accelerating about 1% from the previous quarter. Including workers' compensation, renewal rates were up 6% overall, in line with the previous quarter. This is our 31st consecutive quarter to report overall renewal rate increases, and we believe we're achieving overall renewal rate increases in excess of prospective loss ratio trends to meet or exceed targeted returns. In addition to renewal pricing, we continue to focus on insured values in our property-related businesses to ensure that our premiums reflect inflationary considerations.
Now, I'd like to turn to slide 9 to review a few highlights from each of our specialty property and casualty business groups. Details are included in our earnings release, so I'll focus on our summary results here. The businesses in the Property and Transportation group achieved an 89 calendar year combined ratio overall in Q1 2024, an improvement of 2 points from the 91 reported in the comparable 2023 period. Q1 2024 gross and net written premiums in this group were 10% and 7% higher, respectively, than the comparable prior year period. Additional crop premium associated with the CRS acquisition, as well as new business opportunities, a favorable rate environment, and strong account retentions in our commercial auto and ocean marine businesses, were the primary drivers of the increase in premiums.
Overall, renewal rates in this group increased approximately 9% on average in Q1 2024, an increase of about 2 points from the previous quarter. And I'm particularly pleased with renewal rates achieved in our commercial auto liability line of business, where rates were up 21%. The businesses in our Specialty Casualty group achieved a strong 89.8 calendar year combined ratio in Q1 2024, 2.3 points higher than the 87.5 reported in the comparable period last year. Cat losses added 2.2 points to the Specialty Casualty group Q1 2024 combined ratio and were the result of a winter storm that affected a large social services account in the northwestern part of the country.
I'm particularly pleased with the continued very strong underwriting margins in our executive liability and workers' comp businesses. Q1 2024 gross and net written premiums increased 3% and 4%, respectively, when compared to the same prior year period. While most of the businesses in this group reported premium growth during Q1, the higher year-over-year premiums resulted primarily from the growth in our excess and surplus lines and excess liability businesses as a result of rate increases and new business opportunities. Higher rates, strong account retention, and new business opportunities in several of our targeted markets businesses contributed to the year-over-year growth to a lesser extent.
Now, renewal pricing for this group, excluding our workers' comp businesses, was up approximately 8% in Q1 and was up about 5% overall, with both measures up about 1% from the renewal pricing in the previous quarter. I'm particularly pleased that we achieved renewal rate increases in excess of 10% in several of our social inflation exposed businesses during the quarter, including our public entity, social services, and excess liability businesses. The Specialty Financial Group continued to achieve excellent underwriting margins and reported an 86.3 combined ratio for Q1 2024, a slight improvement from the comparable period in 2023. Q1 2024, gross and net written premiums were up 26% and 27% respectively when compared to the same 2023 period.
While most businesses in this group reported year-over-year growth, our financial institutions business was the primary driver of the higher premiums, representing a continuation of the growth we reported in both of our lender-placed and residential investor business products in the second half of 2023. Renewal pricing in this group was up approximately 7% in Q1. Well, Craig and I are pleased to report these strong results for Q1, and we're proud of our proven track record of long-term value creation. Our insurance professionals have exercised their specialty property and casualty knowledge and experience to skillfully navigate the marketplace. Our in-house investment team has been both strategic and opportunistic in the management of our $15 billion investment portfolio. We're well-positioned to continue to build long-term value for our shareholders for the remainder of 2024 and beyond.
We'll now open the lines for the Q&A portion of today's call, and then Craig and Brian and I would be happy to respond to your questions.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. To remove yourself from the queue, you may press star one one again. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from the line of Charlie Lederer of Citigroup. Your question, please, Charlie.
Charlie Lederer
Research Analyst and VP, Citigroup
Thank you. Good morning. Wondering if you guys can share more about the reserve development in the quarter, I guess specifically in specialty financial and specialty casualty, just the kind of the moving pieces there. Thanks.
Brian Hertzman
CFO, American Financial Group
Hi, Charlie, this is Brian. So, to talk about the casualty segment first, there's a few things going on there. First of all, we did continue to see favorable development coming out of our workers' comp business, as well as lower severity in our executive liability business. Offsetting that is some increased severity in our excess liability businesses and some increased severity in the social services businesses. When Carl mentioned the lower profitability in the social services businesses, that's coming through prior year development, and it's just on a number of a few claims there. While we don't comment on specific claims, it is over a couple of the more recent accident years.
And then in the financial group, there's a small amount of adverse development there, and that's related to our Innovative Markets business, where we're seeing a little bit of increased severity there. The Innovative Markets business includes some coverages related to complex intellectual property.
Charlie Lederer
Research Analyst and VP, Citigroup
Got it. Okay. And I guess that, that's helpful. I guess just on the, the commercial auto liability pricing increase, if I heard that, that kind of jumped off the page at 21%. I guess, well, I guess, what did that compare to in Q4, and, and, and how should we think about, you know, that earnings through and, you know, impacting your underlying margins and, and Property and Transportation as the year goes on?
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
I definitely think it's a, it's a very positive result. I believe, for all of 2023, it was around 11%, but I believe the Q4, jumped up to around 15% or so. So I definitely like the trend. You know, it's our goal, we have solid underwriting performance for our overall commercial auto, business in the Q1 and, and last year. But the commercial auto liability part of the business isn't where we want it, you know, with a small underwriting loss, in that. So it's our objective to, you know, to lower our overall commercial auto, combined ratio, and particularly, you know, on commercial auto liability. So, you know, achieving rate increases at that level is, very welcome at this point.
Charlie Lederer
Research Analyst and VP, Citigroup
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Michael Zaremski of BMO. Please go ahead, Michael.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Well, great. Good afternoon. If we talk, focus on the Specialty Casualty segment, I, you know, the growth, overall top-line growth has been decelerating, which I guess feels like it makes sense, right? Workers' comp pricing is, you know, as it should be, you know, not great, given how great profitability is. On the other hand, you have some of the other lines of business pricing power appears to be going moving north as, you know, the industries and AFG's reserve releases or, you know, I guess, kind of dissipate a bit. I guess, you know, does this just feel kind of like the cycle is playing out as it, you know, as it does?
You know, the pricing kind of in certain lines are, you know, non-comp, are going in the right direction up because, you know, the industry is seeing that, you know, margins are missing a bit. And I guess just trying to get at, is it kind of, does this spike cycle feel like it's turning the right way? You know, with comp obviously being the, the, I guess also turning the right way, but downwards, given profits.
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Yeah, I think, you know, when you look at the to address the growth side, yeah, the workers' comp part of the business, you know, Q1 premium is roughly flat to up just a little bit. So, you know, when you exclude workers' comp, and that's in the specialty casualty segment, we're growing about 6%. I've talked about in the past on the social inflation-exposed businesses, as I just mentioned, really glad to see that we're getting, you know, double-digit price increase on, you know, a number of those businesses, which is a real positive.
But, I think because of the claims environment, you know, in a lot of those lines, our guys are trying to position us for continued success, regardless of, you know, the social inflation, that's going on. I think I've talked in the past of, you know, in certain businesses like public sector, substantially increasing the retentions, you know, over which we're writing business in the municipal pools and increasing, you know, moving up the towers, some with smaller limits and some of our, you know, our excess liability businesses and that.
So, you know, our guys are those businesses, you know, the excess liability businesses have been very profitable for us, but our guys are trying to position us for continued success there going forward in this kind of environment, in that. We continue to be very pleased with the, you know, overall workers' comp results in Q1. So, you know, that's a positive, in that.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Okay, that's helpful. And maybe a follow-up, just to stay on workers' comp, given it's, you know, a good part of your business that's been remained very profitable. You know, is there, you know, when we look at the profitability-
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Mike, uh-
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Yep, sorry.
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Yeah, I might mention, you know, one, you know, one other, you know, in the, the crop business, we're happy with the, you know, right now it's very early, but, the crop year is starting out solid. Plantings of corn and soybeans are proceeding at a pace that exceeds the last five-year average. While, you know, the US Drought Monitor, when you look at that, is better overall than April of last year. And, you know, with reduced drought conditions, across much of the Western Corn Belt, where some of the drought problems existed last year. Despite the, you know, the rainfall, we also don't have significant concerns about floods or above average preventative planning type of claims, in that.
Corn and soybean prices have been very stable, which is good. And, I'm being told that the winter wheat business is, you know, seems to be performing, you know, much better, potentially much better than what it was last year. So, like, extremely early, but like the way we're starting out there on a pretty, a very significant business for us.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
And the winter wheat, and I did have a follow-up on workers' comp. The winter wheat as a percentage of your portfolio, if you can remind us?
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
I think it's maybe 8%, you know, or something like that.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Okay.
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
I think, I think all wheat is maybe 10% or something around that, I bet.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Okay. And if I may, my follow-up was on workers' comp, which is a big and profitable business for you all. If we just, you know... And when we look at just overall industry trends versus American Financial Group last year, you know, your workers' comp business was extremely profitable, but much less profitable, year-over-year. And I'm looking at, on a combined ratio basis, and your reserve releases were still, you know, high, but just decelerated. And the industry actually kind of became more, you know, showed an improvement, which was a surprise.
But, just curious, you know, specific to your book, is there, when you reflect on what the actions you took in 2023, are some of those just due to the nature of your book, maybe being more concentrated in certain states, that your experience was very different than it has been relative to the industry?
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
I'm not sure there's, you know, that significant, you know, of a difference in that. We continued to have great results last year. Our Q1 results are continue to be excellent, you know, for workers' comp. I think in our Summit business, our Strategic Comp business, our high deductible business, and National Interstate's workers' comp are all performing very well. Our California business is the part of the business that has an underwriting loss, both last year and in the Q1. So, that's a relatively smaller part of our workers' comp business in that. But I suppose that, you know, that could have some impact. So we're getting a good start, have excellent comp results in the Q1.
We do think that the profitability, you know, won't be as good as the previous year. One reason, you know, is the 15% rate decline in Florida, which is a significant state for, you know, one of our large comp subsidiaries, Summit.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
That's very helpful. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of C. Gregory Peters of Raymond James. Please go ahead.
[Analyst] (Raymond James)
Analyst, Raymond James
Hey, good morning. This is Sid on for Greg. Just wanted to follow up on the growth in the specialty financial. In the prepared remarks, you highlighted the financial institutions, but curious if you could provide a little bit more information on what you're seeing as attractive in that area of your business. Feels like there's been a step change in growth, and just trying to get a sense if we should expect this to continue.
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
I think we expect, we expect solid growth this year. I think Q1 was, was very strong, in that. I think, you know, different companies talk about leaning into the property opportunities. This is a business that we've done very well over a long period of time with, significant underwriting profitability. With, pricing going up 9%, with, an industry, that's focused on getting the proper insured values. You know, there are states like Florida and, a number of other states that, are moving to, anybody doing this business, making sure that things are insured to replacement cost value, not just the, the, principal balance.
Replacement cost value could be appraised value, or it could be what's called last known coverage replacement cost, which would have been, you know, maybe somebody's last homeowner's policy, in that that was written. So, both price and, you know, getting, proper insured value, competitively, you know, there have been a number of competitors that have faltered and that have allowed us to pick up significant accounts, one in particular last year that, you know, we're continuing to benefit from. We'll see if we—you know, this is a lumpy business in that, you know, when you pick up an account or lose an account, you know, it can have a decent impact on your overall, it comes in lumps.
So, we're hoping that we continue to have some opportunity to pick up maybe some additional accounts. By the same token, you know how, what our thoughts are on, business that's too catastrophically exposed. So if there are accounts that, you know, we don't think are performing or have too much catastrophe exposure, there may be, you know, we may decide not to go forward with some. So, bottom line is, we're pleased with how this business is starting out, very profitable, really good growth, above the price increase and insured value, momentum that we're getting. And, you know, we're - I think we're excited about, the business.
[Analyst] (Raymond James)
Analyst, Raymond James
Okay, thanks. And then, as my follow-up, in the press release, I believe you said the returns in the alternative investment portfolio exceeded expectations for the quarter, and I know you're not providing detailed guidance anymore, but just curious if the Q1 results change your view on the expected performance of the portfolio for this year, or if the 6% annualized return is still the right bogey to use for 2024?
Craig Lindner
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Sure. This, this is Craig. On our last conference call, when we talked about assumptions that went into our plan, you know, we talked about a 6% assumption on total return on alternatives for the year, and that was made up of a low single digit return on our multifamily properties, which account for about half of that portfolio, and a stronger return on the other investments. And what I would say is multifamily is performing pretty much in line with our expectations, or pretty much in line with, you know, what we were kind of expecting to see when we guided to or said that we were using a low single digit return on that piece.
I don't think we changed our thoughts on that, given the outlook for the balance of the year on multifamily. We got off to a very good start. We had very good returns on the balance of the alternative portfolio, but as you know, that can be pretty lumpy. I think we did benefit from the very strong market in Q4 2023 and the calendar year 2023.
You know, we report the returns and marks on a quarter delayed basis. And so I think in the Q1, we benefited from the very strong market last year. It's early in the year, hard to predict what the market's going to do the balance of the year. So I-- at this point in time, we would not change the assumed 6% return for the year.
[Analyst] (Raymond James)
Analyst, Raymond James
Okay, thanks for the answers.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Andrew Anderson of Jefferies. Your question, please, Andrew.
Andrew Andersen
Equity Research VP, Jefferies
Hey, good morning. In the press release, you pointed to improved profitability on workers' comp. Am I correct in thinking that is due to stronger releases year-over-year and not due to the underlying loss ratio? And maybe with that, could you touch on the seasonality of perhaps how 2023s workers' comp developed on a quarterly basis?
Brian Hertzman
CFO, American Financial Group
So the combined ratio, accident or combined ratio was fairly similar in workers' comp quarter-over-quarter, as well as development. So there was a little bit of growth in workers' comp this year, but the underlying loss ratios were similar in that business. There can be some lumpiness in the development, but this in the Q1 of 2024, it was similar to the Q1 of 2023.
Andrew Andersen
Equity Research VP, Jefferies
Okay. And-
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
I don't think our press release said we had an increased, you know, margins there. I think it just said we did well, and I think that's what my earlier comment was, is that, you know, we had strong quarter.
Andrew Andersen
Equity Research VP, Jefferies
Okay, thank you. And then, maybe looking at some Schedule P accident year picks for other liability, claims made seem to improve year-over-year, and occurrence was kind of flat year-over-year for accident year 2023. I guess I would have thought there'd be maybe a little bit more conservatism just given the loss trend environment, but can you kind of help us think through these picks here?
Brian Hertzman
CFO, American Financial Group
Sure. So on the general liability occurrence, I think it's important to know that there could be changes in mix of business, and we also have been getting significant rate increases there. And then in some of, like, our excess businesses, we've also been looking at higher attachment points and higher deductibles. So, so there's really a change of mix of business happening there that, that kind of mutes the impact on the loss pick changes. In the claims made, we tend to be conservative early on, and then that sets us up for more chances of favorable development there.
Andrew Andersen
Equity Research VP, Jefferies
Okay, thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Meyer Shields of Keefe, Bruyette & Woods. Please go ahead, Meyer.
Meyer Shields
Managing Director, Keefe, Bruyette & Woods
Great, thanks. I think earlier, Carl, in your comments, you talked about 20%+ rate increases in commercial auto, and I'm wondering how we should think about that impacting demand for captive solutions as opposed to maintaining the same insurance programs companies have had?
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
I don't think it probably has that big of an impact one way or the other. I mean, you know, the whole marketplace is struggling with social inflation on the commercial auto liability side, and, you know, the market is allowing, you know, increases. Now, you know, on specific captive accounts, if the experience is better, then, you know, it wouldn't be the 21%. You know, there's probably some parts, some accounts, and some businesses that got lower price increases and those that haven't had great results, higher.
Meyer Shields
Managing Director, Keefe, Bruyette & Woods
Okay. So then, I guess where I'm going with this is to just infer that as those rate increases earn in, the improving underwriting profit should basically emerge in the typical fashion instead of being sort of offset by clients retaining significantly more risk.
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Yeah. You know, again, it's our goal to improve the commercial auto liability combined ratios, you know, over the next year or 2, and hence, you know, having a stronger overall commercial auto, you know, results. That's. You know, as I mentioned in some of the specialty casualty lines, we're a very underwriting profit-driven company. I mean, on commercial auto, we're probably outperforming, you know, the market by 5 or 6 points at least, and, you know, we're serious about getting the right returns, you know, on that business.
So if anything, on that part of the business, I'd say our guys are, you know, serious on getting the price and terms changes and the selection of business that achieves our goal, you know, of improving things over the next year or two. So definitely our guys would be, you know, more focused on improving that result than growing a ton right now.
Meyer Shields
Managing Director, Keefe, Bruyette & Woods
Okay, perfect. If I can switch gears briefly, is the growth in specialty financial likely to impact the amount of reinsurance that you want to carry for the rest of the year?
Carl Lindner III
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Definitely! That's something that, you know, we, as that business has grown, that, you know, we definitely are monitoring. I think, in fact, I believe we're looking at, you know, purchasing some gap insurance to cover the gap between our underlying cat tower and the catastrophe bond that we have.
Craig Lindner
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Okay, perfect. Thank you very much.
Operator
Thank you. Once again, to ask a question, please press star one one on your telephone. Again, that's star one one on your telephone to ask a question. Our next question comes from the line of Charlie Lederer of Citigroup. Your question, please, Charlie.
Charlie Lederer
Research Analyst and VP, Citigroup
Hey, thanks. Just one follow-up. You mentioned the Alternative Markets business a little bit. We've heard about certain specialty peers kind of scaling it back after experiencing losses there. I know it's relatively small dollars for you, but curious if you can share whether your thoughts have changed on that business?
Brian Hertzman
CFO, American Financial Group
I assume you're referring to the Innovative Markets business, where we talked about having the-
Charlie Lederer
Research Analyst and VP, Citigroup
Yeah, I misspoke. I said alternative. Yeah, sorry, Innovative Markets, the IP business.
Brian Hertzman
CFO, American Financial Group
So in that business, we're evaluating the opportunities there, and some of the particular programs that have those losses are things that we're no longer offering new coverages in.
Charlie Lederer
Research Analyst and VP, Citigroup
Okay, thank you.
Brian Hertzman
CFO, American Financial Group
Charlie, while we have you, your question earlier about prior year development in the specialty cas, I think it's important also when you're looking at that, to put it in context of where we're coming from in those results. So when you look at the businesses that we had some adverse development in, those are still very profitable businesses for us. For example, for the full year 2023, most of our more social inflation exposed businesses had a calendar year underwriting profit, despite some of the noise there, and only one of them had a return on equity that was in double digits. In fact, when you look at our excess and surplus businesses overall, all three of those had calendar year ROEs above 20% in 2023.
So I thought it might be just good to remember when you're thinking about some of the lumps in prior development, that those are in businesses that are generally very profitable over a long number of years.
Charlie Lederer
Research Analyst and VP, Citigroup
Great. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Michael Zaremski of BMO. Your question please, Michael.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Oh, great, thanks. Just a quick follow-up, probably for Craig, but on the real estate returns, you know, I guess I probably should know this, but I don't. I don't think we all fully appreciate it. Is it a mark to market there, or how does that work? I think we appreciate how private equity works and, you know, sometimes the lag and how the private equity firms mark that, which I think are third parties, but can you remind us how the marks are created on your real estate portfolio? Thanks.
Craig Lindner
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Sure. It is similar to the private equity investments in that the general partners in our multifamily with our multifamily investments review the valuation on a quarterly basis and mark them to market on a quarterly basis.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Okay, got it. So the, you know, the interest rate, so it's, you know. So just as a follow-up, could there be, historically, has there been more volatility on the PE or the real estate? If there's a way to kind of just high level size up whether, you know, we should maybe be thinking about there, maybe there can be some lumpy quarters that actually come from real estate, whereas I thought it usually came from private equity.
Craig Lindner
Co-CEO, American Financial Group
Yeah, I mean, if you look over a long period of time, actually, the multifamily returns have been very predictable. We obviously have been in a somewhat unusual environment here the last 6, 9 months with the very large increase in interest rates. The operating income of the multifamily properties continues very strong. We're very pleased with the performance, but cap rates have moved up because of an increase in interest rates.
Michael Zaremski
Senior Equity Research Analyst and Managing Director, BMO
Okay, that's all I have. Appreciate it.
Operator
Thank you. I would now like to turn the conference back to Diane Weidner for closing remarks. Ma'am?
Diane Weidner
VP of Investor Relations, American Financial Group
Thank you all for joining us today as we discussed our Q1 results. We look forward to talking to you again next quarter and hope you all have a great day.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
